\section*{Inversion in Two Dimensions.}


In this case if $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ represent the distances of corresponding
 points from $O, e$ and $e^{\prime}$ the total electrification of a body, $S$ and $S^{\prime \prime}$
 superficial elements, $V$ and $V^{\prime}$ solid elements, $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{\prime}$ surface
densities, $\rho$ and $\rho^{\prime}$ volume densities, $\phi$ and $\psi^{\prime}$ corresponding poten
tials,

$$\begin{align*}
& r^{\prime}=\frac{\grave{s}^{\prime}}{S}=\frac{a^{2}}{r^{2}}=\frac{r^{\prime 2}}{a^{2}}, \quad V^{\prime}=\frac{a^{4}}{r^{4}}=\frac{r^{\prime 4}}{a^{4}} \\
& \frac{e^{\prime}}{e}=1, \quad \frac{\sigma^{\prime}}{\sigma}=\frac{r^{2}}{a^{2}}=\frac{a^{2}}{r^{\prime 2}}, \quad \frac{\rho^{\prime}}{\rho}=\frac{r^{4}}{a^{4}}=\frac{a^{4}}{r^{4}} \tag{7}
\end{align*}$$

and since by hypothesis $\phi^{\prime}$ is got from $\phi$ by expressing
 the old variables in terms of the new, $\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{\phi}=1$.


Example II.-Electric Images in Two Dimensions.

189.] Let $A$ be the centre of a circle of radius $A Q=b$ at zero
 potential, and let $E$ be a charge at $A$,
 then the potential at any point $P$ is

$$\begin{equation*}
\phi=2 E^{\prime} \log \frac{b}{A P^{\prime}} ; \tag{8}
\end{equation*}$$

and if the circle is a section of a
 hollow conducting cylinder, the surface
density at any point $Q$ is $-\frac{E}{2 \pi} \frac{}{b}$.


\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_11_28_e96c2f916abc8f617e8eg-326.jpg?height=218&width=355&top_left_y=900&top_left_x=773}
\captionsetup{labelformat=empty}
\caption{Fig. 17.}
\end{figure}


Invert the system with respect to a point $O$, making

$$A O=m b, \text { and } \alpha^{2}=\left(m^{2}-1\right) b^{2} ;$$

then the circle inverts into itself and we have a charge at $A^{\prime}$
 equal to that at $A$, where

$$A A^{\prime}=\frac{b}{m} .$$


The density at $Q^{\prime}$ is

$$-\underset{2 \pi b}{E} \frac{b^{2}-\left.\bar{A} \bar{A}^{\prime}\right|^{2}}{A^{\prime} Q^{\prime 2}},$$

and the potential at any point $P^{\prime}$ within the circle is

$$\begin{align*}
\psi^{\prime}=\phi & =2 E(\log b-\log A P), \\
& =2 E\left(\log O P^{\prime}-\log A^{\prime} P^{\prime}-\log m\right) . \tag{9}
\end{align*}$$


This is equivalent to the potential arising from a combination
 of a charge $E$ at $A^{\prime}$, and a charge $-E$ at $O$, which is the image
 of $A^{\prime}$ with respect to the circle. The imaginary charge at $O$ is
 thus equal and opposite to that at $A^{\prime}$.
